description.zh: 一把已经击发的信号枪、一张烧焦的信托修正案，以及四个各执一词的人，让暴风雨后的那个夜晚变成霍华德·维尔留下的最终清算。

title.en: The Night Daniel Mercer Returned Before the Lies Devoured the Old House
title.zh: 在谎言彻底吞噬老宅前，丹尼尔·默瑟归来的那个夜晚

summary.en: On the storm-darkened night Daniel Mercer returns to Marlowe Estate, a discharged flare gun and a burned trust amendment force four members of a broken household to reveal what each of them hid after Howard’s death.
summary.zh: 暴风雨后的夜晚，丹尼尔·默瑟回到马罗庄园。一把已经击发的信号枪和一张烧焦的信托修正案残片，迫使这个破碎家庭里的四个人交代霍华德死后各自隐瞒的秘密。

warning.en: Fiction. Contains a flare-gun discharge, minor blood and injury, intense family confrontation, grief, financial wrongdoing and emotional manipulation.
warning.zh: 虚构故事。包含信号枪击发、轻微流血与受伤、激烈家庭冲突、丧亲、财务不当行为及情感操控情节。

en: ## Chapter One
The scratches on her hairline had stopped bleeding, and a thin red line was hidden among the brown hair.
“I brought her here.” Claire broke the ice.
Daniel’s fingers tightened on Veronica’s wrist and relaxed slightly.
Ruth stared at her in astonishment.
Veronica turned slightly sideways and looked over her shoulder at Daniel. The expression on her face changed extremely slightly, even showing a hint of creepy softness.
“You really don’t know anything, do you?”
Daniel had a free hand and pulled open a bar chair next to the island.
“Sit down.”
Veronica glanced at the chair.
“I told you to sit down.”
She obeyed. Daniel still clamped one of her wrists tightly. At the same time, Ruth picked up the flare gun, stretched out her arm and placed it on the farthest countertop like a hot potato.
“Open it,” Daniel ordered.
Ruth looked at him apprehensively.
“That flare gun. Check to see if it’s empty.”
“I...I don’t know how to do it.”
“There’s a release button next to the trigger guard.”
Her hands were shaking so much that the flare gun made a sharp and crisp sound on the marble countertop. Claire walked over and took it from Ruth.
“Give it to me.” Daniel said solemnly.
“I know how to do it.” Claire replied.
“How do you know?”
Claire pressed the release button, and the gun barrel popped open, revealing a fired aluminum cartridge case.
Daniel looked at her.
“The Lake District Safety Course,” she explained, “it was you who forced me to take it twice.”
Ruth walked across the kitchen and picked up the cordless phone hanging by the pantry door. She pressed the call button and listened for a while.
“There is no blind tone, the line is broken.”
“The storm yesterday knocked out the outside line.” Daniel said, “Use my cell phone to call.”
“Your phone is in the living room.” Claire answered.
“How do you know?”
“I just saw it.”
Daniel looked past her. His phone was lying quietly on the edge of the light-colored carpet, the screen dark.
“Go get it,” he said to Ruth.

Veronica sat upright on the bar stool, one wrist still in Daniel’s grasp. She didn’t struggle. The satin sleeve slipped down, revealing a bruise on his forearm. Daniel didn’t remember that he had hurt her, but he subconsciously relaxed his grip.
Ruth came back with her cell phone.
“The screen is broken.”
“It was broken before.”
“It won’t light up no matter how hard I press it.”
Daniel took it, pressed the side button, and tapped it twice in his palm. No response.
“Use Claire’s phone,” he said.
Claire stared down at the floor.
“Where’s the phone?”
“In your office.”
“What is it doing in my office?”
The corners of Veronica’s lips curved into a faint sneer.
It wasn’t until this moment that Daniel truly understood the outline of tonight’s farce.

His eyes moved away from Claire and fell on the broken vase. It was just a plain white ceramic vase, hand-painted with slender blue reeds. It sat by the fireplace for several years. Even after Howard Vale died and the house became less like a home and more like an expensive corpse waiting to be dissected, Ruth insisted on changing it with flowers every Monday.
And among the ceramic shards lay something darker than the carpet.
A thick piece of parchment with badly burnt edges.
Veronica noticed that his gaze was fixed.
Daniel let go of her wrist.

He strode to the fireplace and knelt down. There is still residual warmth on the stone slab. The flare carved a black hole in the floor of the fireplace and even melted a small patch of carpet. He carefully picked up the scrap of paper with two fingers.
Only three words on the paper were barely legible.
Trust Amendment.
He stood up.
Claire raised her chin slightly, even though her face was already as pale as paper.
Daniel held up the charred fragment.
“What exactly did you take from my office?”
No one answered.
“Claire.”
Her thumbs rubbed the seams of her sweater.
“I found out last week.”
“What did you find?”
“You know it.”
“I want to hear it from your own mouth.”
“Howard’s Amendment.”
Ruth let out a low cry in her throat and slumped down on the nearest bar stool.
Daniel stared at her. She avoided his sight.

Veronica placed her hands flat on her knees. She seemed to have regained her condescending composure, but Daniel saw through her forced pretense—her fingers gripped the satin fabric too hard, and the rise and fall of her chest seemed short and labored.
“You swore to me that this thing didn’t exist at all.” She said coldly.
Daniel was still staring at Ruth.
“I asked you point-blank after Howard died. You stood in the library, looked me in the eye and told me there were absolutely no follow-up documents.”
“There is absolutely no follow-up document that is 'legally binding',” Daniel retorted.
“That’s not what you said at the time.”
“When he signed that thing, he was already so sick that he was delirious!”
“He was indeed dying when he signed it, but that’s not the same thing as being 'delirious'.”
Claire took a step closer to the fireplace. Daniel subconsciously stood in front of the burned piece of paper.
“You went through my filing cabinet.” Daniel asked his daughter.
“You hid it.”
“That office is locked!”
“I know where you hid the spare key.”
“Of course you do.”
This sentence was blurted out with a strong sense of sarcasm, and even the father and daughter themselves were stung.
Claire stared at him: “What do you mean?”
“It means that you have been treating this house as a playground. All the rules apply to others, except for you.”
“I learned this from you.”
Ruth closed her eyes in pain.

The sneer on Veronica’s lips disappeared. The air in the room seemed to freeze. Through the huge floor-to-ceiling windows, the afterglow of the evening spreads out narrow strips of silver light on Marrow Lake. A motorboat passed by on the other side. The distance was too far, and the people on the boat had no way of knowing that someone had just fired a fatal signal flare indoors in this prestigious Weir Manor.
Daniel folded the scrap of paper in half.
“Where’s the rest?”
“Burned to ashes by a flare,” Veronica said.
Claire shook her head.
Daniel turned to her.
“The original was not in that vase at all,” she said.
Veronica stood up abruptly, the legs of the bar chair scraping against the floor.
Daniel immediately stepped between them.
“Sit down.”
“She lied to me!” Veronica screamed.
“So you pointed the flare gun at her?!”
“I’m aiming for the vase!”
“You fired into a room! There were three living people standing not ten feet away!”
“She told me the documents were hidden inside!”
“So you think setting it on fire is the most rational way to deal with it?”
“I didn’t mean to burn it!”
Daniel pointed to the blackened base of the fireplace.
“Then what do you want to do?”
Veronica opened her mouth, but was stuck.
Claire answered for her.
“She thought the documents were sealed inside the vase.”
Ruth looked at the pile of fragments in shock: “Sealed?”
“She decided Howard had sealed the signed copy inside.”
“Why would he do such a ridiculous thing?”
“Because Veronica told me that Howard had been guarding against my dad and hiding things secretly.”
Daniel turned sharply to Veronica.
“What the hell are you talking about to her?”
“Mostly the truth.”
“Mostly.” Daniel chewed the word.
“I told her, Howard has lost trust in you a long time ago.”
“When Howard thinks he is a good person, he trusts the whole world; when he thinks he is a smart person, he trusts no one. You know this better than anyone else.”
## Chapter Two
Veronica’s face tightened.
Daniel thought, finally the secret was revealed. She’s not crazy, at least not yet. This is malice with a clear purpose.

Veronica moved into Marlowe Manor three years before Howard’s death. At first, she was just a consultant for the East Wing Charitable Foundation; later, she became a “female companion” that everyone knew but never mentioned. She would attend high-profile dinners in silk evening gowns and review grant proposals barefoot at the breakfast table. Howard, seventy-one years old and newly widowed, stubbornly declared to the servants that their personal relationships had nothing to do with the running of the estate.
Veronica also played along with this performance until the relationship became involved with “The Will.”

Daniel was disgusted with her even before he had any definite reason. Now he dared to admit it in private. She was encroaching on space in this house too quickly. Without saying hello, she opened his bottle of red wine and moved the books around on the bookshelf according to her own weird logic. She affectionately called Howard “H” in front of employees. She spoke to Daniel as if his fifteen years of painstaking management of the manor were nothing more than a lengthy administrative error.
Later, Howard fell ill and Veronica stayed.

She memorized all his medication orders, slept in the nursing chair next to his bed all night, and argued with the nurse on the phone. When Daniel couldn’t even feed him a sip of water, she always had a way of coaxing Howard into eating half a piece of toast. No matter what kind of person she was, she was never absent during those most difficult days.
This made the remaining paper in Daniel’s hand weigh as much as a thousand pounds.
“I want to get Claire’s phone.” He took a deep breath.
“In the bottom drawer of your desk.” Veronica said coldly.
Daniel didn’t look at her: “Why are you there?”
“In case she calls you for help.”
Claire’s voice was as calm as water: “I put it in myself.”
“Why?”
“Because I know you so well, you will definitely turn everything tonight into a 'hero saves daughter' drama.”
“You were hiding behind the island, and someone was holding a heavy candlestick to hit you!”
“She didn’t hit me with that.”
“She scratched you!”
“I hit it on the cabinet handle and scratched it myself.”
Ruth glanced at the injury on Claire’s hairline.
“As Miss Hale was lifting the candlestick, I pulled Claire down,” the housekeeper testified, “and she hit the drawer handle.”
Daniel immediately turned his finger on Ruth: “When I called back from Milwaukee this morning, you clearly told me that everything was peaceful at home!”
“I was saying, it was a really quiet moment.”
Daniel couldn’t help but let out an extremely unpleasant sneer.
Veronica looked on with cold eyes. “That’s the thing about this house, isn’t it? Every answer is literally the truth.”

Daniel walked to the counter and picked up the flare gun. The barrel was still open and the aluminum cartridge casing was clearly visible. He closed the barrel of the gun, stuffed it into the wall cabinet above the refrigerator, and removed the key from the cabinet door.
“Ruth, look at her.”
Ruth’s eyebrows rose.
“Look at me?” Veronica felt a little ridiculous.
“Ruth, if she tries to get near any drawers, doors, heavy objects, or anything that could ignite, tell me immediately.”
“Then what should I do after I tell you?”
“No need to do anything.”
“Finally,” Veronica sneered, “a perfect plan worthy of the title of butler.”
Daniel ignored her.

He walked into the living room to get his cell phone, even though he knew it was a piece of scrap metal. One corner of the screen was completely shattered. He pressed the power button firmly, and a faint green line flashed on the screen, then fell into dead silence again. On the carpet nearby lay his overnight bag, unzipped. This was what he had thrown away when he heard the scream just now.
The glass door behind him was wide open.

Through the door, he could have a panoramic view of the kitchen: Claire stood by the fireplace, Ruth sat awkwardly on the stool, and Veronica sat back down, her hands firmly in the open. This picture is like a weird family photo that no one wants to click the shutter on.
Daniel picked up his travel bag and walked to the console in the entrance hall. His laptop is inside. He turned on the computer, pressed the power button, and the screen lit up.
Wireless network shows: No connection.
“The router is out of action,” he shouted.
No one responded.
He took the notebook back to the kitchen.
“The security panel has cellular backup,” he said as he walked, “and I can send an SOS signal from there.”
“It was flashing red just now,” Ruth reminded.
“Where?”
“In the equipment corridor.”
Daniel hurried through the kitchen. Sure enough, the security panel next to the laundry room flashed a dazzling red light. System failure. Cellular module is offline.
He entered the repair code. The failure log shows that at 3:12 this afternoon, there was a complete loss of external signal.
He knelt down and checked the modem in the cabinet below. The power cord was unplugged.
Daniel stared at the plug.
Claire appears at the end of the corridor.
“I didn’t pull it out.”
“I haven’t asked you yet.”
“The look in your eyes already asked.”
“Go back to the kitchen.”
“Dad.”
“Go back!”
She stood stubbornly.

The equipment hallway is narrow, and the walls are covered with old photos of the house before Howard renovated it. One was taken in the 1950s, when the kitchen still had dark wood cabinets and linoleum floors. Several men with their sleeves rolled up stood where the marble island now stands. Everyone in the photo seems reluctant to be photographed.
Daniel plugged the modem back in. The indicator light on the panel starts to pulse.
“Did Veronica pull it out?” Claire asked.
“I don’t know.”
“It must be her.”
“How do you know?”
“I saw her walk out of here.”
“Before you hid your phone, or after?”
Claire’s lips formed a straight line.
Daniel waited for the router to reconnect. Nothing happened. He disassembled the bottom access panel and suddenly found that the main optical cable outside had been cut off.
He looked back at his daughter.
“Did you see her take the knife?”
“No.”
“Where are the scissors?”
“No.”
“Then you don’t know anything.”
“You’re actually defending her now?!”
“I’m trying to figure out what the hell happened!”
“You can ask me calmly!”
“I’ve been asking you from the second I stepped into the kitchen!”
“You call that an interrogation!”
Daniel slammed the equipment cabinet door with a loud bang that was deafening.
Claire shrank her shoulders in fear.
The flinch lasted less than a second, and she recovered so quickly that if Daniel hadn’t been her father, he might not even have noticed.
He suppressed his anger and lowered his voice.
“Start from the beginning.”
She glanced warily in the direction of the kitchen. “Not in front of her.”
“Okay.”
“Not in front of Ruth either.”
This request itself has revealed too much information.

Daniel looked toward the kitchen. Ruth sat stiffly, her hands folded in her lap. Veronica stared at the corridor like an alert cheetah, obviously aware that some shady secrets were secretly operating away from her.
“Go to the living room.” Daniel ordered.
He walked over first, leaving the choice of whether to follow to Claire.
## Chapter Three
She followed anyway.

Daniel closed one of the glass doors but left the other slightly open to make sure he could hear what was going on in the kitchen. The house was eerily quiet. Even the refrigerator compressor seemed to have stopped humming.
Instead of sitting on the sofa, Claire sat awkwardly on the edge of an armchair.
“Howard’s trust amendment, was it really you who deliberately hid it?” She got straight to the point.
Daniel dropped the scrap metal cell phone on the coffee table.
“This shouldn’t be the beginning of the story.”
“For me, that’s it.”
“Claire.”
“You just have to answer yes or no.”
He looked at the scratches on her forehead and uttered one word heavily: “Yes.”
She blinked blankly.
He had expected a furious accusation, or some sort of triumph in exposing his true colors. However, what appeared on her face was an exhaustion and disappointment that was far beyond her years.
“You keep lying to me and saying she’s lying.”
“What I was saying was that she had no 'enforceable' legal title to the estate.”
“This is just a play on words.”
“Yes.”
“Does mom know about this?”
“I don’t know.”
Claire turned her head and looked out the window at the lake.

The sun had hidden behind a thick layer of clouds, taking away the sparkling luster from the lake. The living room was still bright, but the shadows around the edges of the ceiling had begun to deepen inexorably.
Daniel sat down opposite her.

“Eleven days before Howard died, he signed a proposed amendment. The terms gave Veronica lifetime use of the west wing, an annuity payable annually by the foundation, and a percentage of the estate’s realization should it be sold in the future.”
“What percent?”
“Fifteen percent.”
“But she told me it was 20 percent.”
“On the document I saw, it was fifteen percent.”
“Why don’t you turn this document over to the legal team?”
“This is because Howard’s treating physician at the time clearly questioned whether he still had the cognitive ability to make major financial decisions.”
“Has he been deemed incapacitated?”
“The doctor has not made a final conclusion.”
“Then why did you withhold the documents?”
“Because two days before signing this document, Howard was furious and accused Ruth of stealing his antique cufflinks! And that pair of cufflinks, he had given to his nephew ten years ago!”
“He’s just old and forgetful.”

“Not only is he forgetful, his mood fluctuates violently every hour! He promised the same famous painting to three people! He even tried to transfer the ownership of the houseboat on the lake to a worker who only came to clean the gutters once!”
“So you’re acting as a substitute, deciding for him which of his last wishes will count and which of them will be invalidated?”
“I’m just temporarily sealing the document until we can confirm its validity through legal means.”
“How long have you been keeping it sealed?”
Daniel was silent.
Claire nodded slowly. “A whole six months.”
“I admit, I should have gone through the procedure.”
“You put it in the shredder?”
“No.”
“Then where is it?”
“In the fireproof safe in my office.”
Claire rubbed her hands together vigorously.
“Then what was that I took?”
“A copy.”
“You already knew I took it?”
“I found out last week that the folder had been tampered with.”
“But you didn’t even ask me a question.”
“I thought Ruth had been in there.”
Claire gave him an utterly ridiculous look.
“Of course you think so.”
“What do you mean?”
“It means that in your eyes, you will always give priority to doubting the subordinate who is paid to do things, rather than the person you claim you love.”

Daniel almost blurts out that “love” only makes the price of doubt more expensive, not cheaper. But he choked it back because it sounded too much like the hypocritical sermon Howard would deliver after two glasses of red wine.
“Why did you contact Veronica?”
“She was the one who contacted me first.”
“How did you get in touch?”
“Send an email.”
“Why does she have your email address?”
“You can just look for it, it’s not difficult.”
“What did she say in the email?”
“She said Howard signed a document that you had secretly withheld. She even included a photo of the signature page.”
Daniel leaned forward sharply. “Show me that picture.”
“My phone is in your office.”
“So, it was after she contacted you that you went through my filing cabinet?”
“Yes.”
“Then you lured the wolf into the house and recruited her into your home?!”
“She originally lived here!”
“She should have moved out yesterday!”
“But she came back this afternoon.”
“Who let her in?”
Claire lowered her head.
Daniel closed his eyes in pain.
“You gave her the code to the gate.”
“I thought we could sit down and talk it out.”
“Going straight to someone who’s hiding top-secret legal documents?”
“I want to tell you clearly!”
“What shocking secrets do you expect her to tell you that you don’t already know?”
“I hope she can tell me why you are so afraid of her.”
“I’m not afraid of her at all.”
“You should be afraid.”
Daniel turned to look at the kitchen.
Veronica was still sitting there. Ruth had taken a dish towel from the drawer and was folding it into smaller and smaller squares.
“Did Veronica cut the network cable?”
“Yes.”
“You just said you didn’t see anything in her hand.”
“I really didn’t see it. She told me personally that she cut the thread.”
“When did you say that?”
“After Ruth caught us in your office.”
“What were you doing in the office?”
“Find the original.”
“Did you find it?”
Claire shook her head.
“Then why does she believe the original is in that vase?”
“Because I told her.”
“Are you crazy? Why?”
“Because she was holding that heavy brass candlestick in her hand!”
Daniel stood up suddenly, walked to the window, and pressed his palms heavily against the cold glass.
“Tell me exactly what happened, word for word.”
Claire spoke slowly at first.

Veronica arrived just after three o’clock. She even wore the same couture dress she wore to last night’s charity dinner. She claimed her hotel reservation was expired and Daniel cold-bloodedly withheld two of her suitcases that were still in the West Wing. Claire believed it and let her in. Ruth was upstairs changing the sheets.
But Veronica didn’t pick up any suitcases at all.
She went straight to Daniel’s office.

Claire followed closely because she was brought in for the showdown. Claire deftly opened the door with the brass key hidden at the bottom of the console table. Veronica obviously also knew about the existence of this key, which was what Howard told her before he died.
In the office, Claire used Daniel’s spare set of labeled keys to open the locked filing cabinet. She found the exact folder where she had seen a copy of the amendment last week.
It was empty inside.

Veronica immediately turned her back, accusing Claire of being a mole sent by Daniel to deliberately arouse the enemy. Claire retorted, accusing Veronica of taking advantage of Howard’s insanity to brainwash him while he was ill. The two of them argued in silence until Ruth suddenly opened the door and came in and saw the large open filing cabinet.
Ruth sternly orders Veronica to get out.
Veronica refuses.
Ruth reached for the phone on her desk. Veronica ripped off the phone cord, rushed into the equipment corridor, and used the scissors on Daniel’s desk to cut off the main optical cable.
“Why didn’t you take the opportunity to run out while she was wreaking havoc?” Daniel was furious.
“I want the truth.”
“You’ve seen the truth! That folder is empty!”
“I want to hear her admit it with my own ears!”
“Hear what Ruth admits?”
“Admit that she worked with you to hide the amendment!”
Daniel turned sharply from the window.
Claire stared at him.
“Did she do it?” she pressed.
“I don’t know what you’re talking about.”
“The look on your face gives you away.”
“All I know is that Ruth knew that Howard signed some messy documents before he died.”
“That’s not a question I asked you at all.”
## Chapter Four
“No.” Daniel replied decisively.
“She didn’t help you hide the documents?”
“No.”
He answered so quickly that he didn’t even have time to cover up.
Claire stood up.
“You’re here again.”
“What’s coming again?”
“They are trying to trick me again with that 'literally correct' shortened version of the truth.”
There was the sound of chairs scraping against the floor in the kitchen.
Veronica raised her voice and her voice penetrated the glass door: “Ask him what’s going on with that 'witness signature page'!”
Daniel’s stomach jerked.
Claire looked at the slightly open glass door in confusion.
“What witness signature page?”
“Stay here and don’t move,” Daniel ordered.
Veronica let out a soft, mocking laugh.
Ruth seemed to retort in a low voice, but her voice was too low to be heard clearly.
Claire didn’t obey and walked straight into the kitchen. Daniel followed.
Veronica was still sitting on the bar stool, but her body was completely turned in Ruth’s direction.
“What good did you do?” Claire asked the housekeeper.
Ruth placed the folded dish towel on the counter. It has been folded into an extremely neat blue and white square smaller than the palm of your hand.
“Miss Hale is just bluffing and trying to scare you.”
“You were there when Howard signed the amendment.”
“Yes.”
“Are you a witness?”
Ruth’s eyes flickered to Daniel.
Veronica caught the look with the precision of a vulture.
“Look,” she said with a sneer, “just this look has exposed the dirty interests in this house.”
Daniel leaned against the island platform and crossed his arms tightly in front of his chest, trying to hide the uncontrollable slight trembling in his hands.
“Tell her, Ruth.”
Ruth looked at him warily: “Tell her which part?”
“The part she asked.”
Ruth pushed the folded towel away.
“Howard did ask me to sign the document as a witness. But I refused.”
“Why?” Claire asked.
“His mind was completely confused that morning.”
“Why are you confused?”
“He took my hand and called me Miriam.”
“Who is Miriam?”
“His first wife.”
Veronica’s voice suddenly became extremely sharp: “He corrected it quickly!”
“That was after I reminded him loudly.”
“He knew exactly what he was signing!”
“You have no right to assert it for him!”
“Before you came in with a glass of water, I had been chatting with him for two full hours!”
“And I have been with him for twenty-six years!”
“You’re just a cleaning servant!”
Ruth’s expression changed.

Daniel had seen countless times how Ruth calmly dealt with the arrogant guests who treated her as invisible, and also saw how she responded gracefully to the trust directors who couldn’t even remember her name but pretended to be polite. She never showed any hint of sullenness. But at this moment, the look in her eyes when she looked at Veronica actually revealed a spine-chilling calmness.
“Yeah,” Ruth said coldly, “I’m responsible for cleaning up all the mess you glamorous parasites leave behind.”
Veronica was actually the first to look away to avoid his sharp edge.
Claire’s eyes flicked back and forth between the two.
“If Ruth didn’t sign as a witness, who did?”
“Two junior employees at the foundation,” Daniel replied, “they signed.”
“Then why does she keep mentioning the missing 'witness signature page'?”
Veronica said quickly:
“Because after Howard’s death, the signed amendment was strangely missing the last page!”
Claire frowned. “But the copy I saw was signed.”

“What you see is a spliced scan that has been tampered with,” Veronica sneered. “The original original document clearly had twelve pages, but the original document handed over to Daniel only had eleven pages.”
Daniel felt like the entire kitchen space was squeezing against him.
Claire turned to him in shock. “Is this true?”
“...It’s true.”
“Where did the last page go?”
“No one knows.”
Ruth stood up suddenly.
Although her movements were still deliberately slow and cautious, Daniel could clearly see the fear rising again in her eyes.

“Howard liked to do this kind of thing in his later years, tearing documents into pieces,” she stammered in defense. “He would jot notes on the backs of various documents, and then carry them around in various rooms.”
Veronica stared at her.
“You told Daniel yourself that the page had been destroyed.”
Ruth seemed to have lost her hearing and was silent.
Daniel lowered his crossed arms.
“When did she ever tell me that?”
“The morning after Howard died.”
“That morning I was with her almost every step of the way to deal with the funeral arrangements!”
“But you weren’t in the laundry room with her.”
Ruth turned and headed toward the storeroom. Daniel strode forward, blocking her path.
“Ruth.”
“I need some water.”
“I’ll pour it for you.”
“I’m not so crippled that I can’t pour a glass of water!”
Although she tried her best to keep her voice steady, her left hand began to tremble violently again uncontrollably.

Daniel took out a glass from the cupboard, filled it with water and handed it to her. Ruth took it without even saying thank you. She downed half the glass, then pressed the glass tightly against her cardigan, as if drawing some strength from it.
Claire followed closely: “Did you destroy the last page?”
“No.”
“Have you seen that page after Howard signed it?”
Ruth stared at the water in the cup.
“...I’ve seen it.”
Veronica stood up.
Daniel pointed at the stool sharply: “Sit down!”
“Don’t even think about it!”
“I told you to sit down!”
“Your flare gun is out of bullets!”
“My ordering you to sit down has nothing to do with that damn gun!”
“In your eyes, everything tonight is only related to that damn flare gun! Because only by biting this point can your hypocritical conscience feel that you are an innocent victim who is blameless!”
Daniel took a step closer, furious.
Claire stepped nimbly between them.
But she didn’t completely block Veronica’s way like Daniel guarding the sink. She found an extremely tricky angle to ensure that both of them were in sight at the same time.
“Everyone stay where you are,” she ordered.
Daniel looked at his daughter in disbelief.
Her voice was not loud, but because of that, her undeniable majesty was irresistible.
Ruth slumped back on her stool. Veronica still stood, but didn’t take another step forward.
Claire pointed to the charred carpet.
“She shot because I lied to her and the witness signature page was hidden in that vase.”
Daniel’s eyes widened.
“You already knew there was a missing page?!”

“I don’t know.”
“You said these four words tonight more times than I have ever heard you say in my entire life.”
“Because I’m already very skilled at it.”
She turned her head and gave him a very complicated look.
He forced himself to swallow a sip of coffee. The coffee has long been bitter and difficult to swallow as it has been simmering on the warming plate.
“I have sent electronic copies of all documents to the trust directors.” He broke the silence.
“I saw it.”
“At the same time, I also formally submitted my resignation to them.”
Claire’s expression changed. “So fast?!”
“Effective immediately.”
“Did you send it on your mobile phone?”
“Use your phone.”
“You submitted your resignation letter in my email APP?!”
“I logged out after posting.”
“That’s not what I’m worried about!”
“I know.”
She shook her head helplessly, and a forced smile appeared on her lips that was uglier than crying.
“Why are you leaving in such a hurry?”

“Because I concealed an extremely critical trust document. Because I seriously neglected my duties and failed to thoroughly investigate the whereabouts of investors' funds despite having sufficient reasons to suspect. And because, if I continue to stay in this position, every decision I make will be infinitely amplified by the outside world and turn into an endless political wrangling about whether I am protecting the foundation or protecting myself from being implicated.”
“Then were you protecting yourself?”
“Yes.”
“What about the foundation?”
“Same.”
“Which one is the real reason?”
Daniel stared at the cloudy coffee in the cup.
“I’m always very adept at switching between these two high-sounding answers at any time, depending on who is questioning me.”
Claire crossed her arms, trying to resist the chill that penetrated her bones.
“Then what are you going to do next?”
“Get a new job.”
“What?”
“After all, I managed this massive property for seventeen years.”
“You’re in charge of Howard.”
“It’s in charge of the foundation.”
“Aren’t they all in the same house?”
“Most of the time it is.”
“If you leave this house, you won’t even know who you are.”
This almost cruel analysis is impossible to refute precisely because it is so objective and pertinent.
“Yeah,” Daniel admitted dryly, “I really don’t know.”
Claire cast her gaze onto the dark lake.
The huge floor-to-ceiling window glass reflected their shadows sitting side by side extremely faithfully, and there was still an extremely subtle physical distance between the two bar chairs.
“I really didn’t want to invite Veronica to hurt anyone.” She said with extreme remorse.
“I know.”
“I naively thought that as long as I could find conclusive evidence, I could force you to confess all the truth to me in person.”
“You can just ask me directly.”
“I asked!”
“When?”
“Last month! I’m asking you in all seriousness why she’s emailing you like a stalker!”
“Then what you’re asking is whether she is extorting money from the manor.”
## Chapter Fifteen
“Then you said without hesitation that she just wanted the money.”
“She does want money.”
“But you most despicably concealed from me that she had a signed copy of the damn amendment in her hand!”
“Yes.”
Claire rubbed her cold hands together vigorously.
“I was extremely desperate to catch you in action.”
Daniel made no attempt to interrupt her and let these sharp words fall in the air.

“I hate myself for having such vicious thoughts,” she continued to accuse with red eyes, “but every time, when you use that carefully packaged 'half-truth' to deal with me, you are mercilessly mocking me for believing your other 'half-truth' and making me look like a complete fool.”
“You’re not stupid.”
“But that doesn’t change the fact that I was fooled by you.”
“Yes.”
She stared at him.

He didn’t ask for her forgiveness. The overwhelming urge to be forgiven is real, even with a shameful childishness. But he exercised extreme restraint, because once he begged, it would be extremely selfish to force the burden of “forgive him and make his conscience feel better” on his daughter’s shoulders.

“I’m sorry.” He said softly, “I apologize not because you discovered the truth in such a tragic way. But because... I not only told you extremely poor lies, but I also deceived you into believing it at some point. It’s both.”
The corners of Claire’s mouth twitched painfully.
“This line sounds like it has been rehearsed in front of the mirror countless times.”
“I didn’t rehearse.”
“It sounds like the PR rhetoric you crafted in the corner while I was being questioned repeatedly by the police in the kitchen.”
“That’s what ran through my mind when Veronica pulled the trigger of the flare gun.”
“Was it before you fell to the ground in fear, or after?”
“Probably at the same time.”
She let out a very short wry laugh, and then suddenly covered her face with her hands.
That wry smile instantly twisted into an extremely suppressed, heart-rending sob.
Daniel instinctively wanted to reach out and hold her in his arms.
But before his fingers touched her, he stopped abruptly.
Claire slowly lowered her hands.
“You can do it.” She said with a thick nasal voice.
With the utmost care and restraint he put an arm around her shoulders. His shoulder hurt like it was on fire. But he endured it and didn’t move at all.
They cuddled together until Ruth returned to the kitchen.

She changed into a very plain gray bathrobe and a pair of old slippers. Without her iconic blue woolen cardigan and dark uniform skirt, she no longer looked like the iron-fisted housekeeper who had ruled the mansion for decades, but just a tired woman who had been completely drained of energy under the pale midnight light.
“I made some sandwiches.” She came over with a plate.
Daniel looked at the plate in her hand in astonishment.
“Why?”
“Because none of us had a damn bite of dinner after such a crazy night.”
Claire wiped the tears on her face haphazardly. “What kind of stuffing?”
“Ham.”
“I gave up ham a long time ago.”
“You obviously ate like a wolf last Christmas.”
“I quit smoking completely in March this year.”
Ruth stared at her speechlessly.
“Why?!”
“Because I watched an extremely cruel animal protection documentary.”
Ruth slammed the plate onto the counter.
“It also has cheese stuffed in it.”
“Thank you.”
Daniel silently picked up a ham sandwich and chewed it.
Ruth sat down opposite them.

For several minutes, no one spoke except for the sound of chewing. Claire tore off the crust with great care and folded it neatly on the edge of the plate - this was actually a bad habit she had had since she was a child, but she had refused to admit it as an adult. Daniel ate so fast that he almost choked. Ruth just held a cup of hot tea and stared blankly at the dark window.
“Where do you plan to go in the future?” Daniel broke the silence.
Ruth turned and looked at him. “Go upstairs and sleep.”
“I’m asking after this manor is completely sold.”
“I’m going to Pennsylvania to join my sister.”
“Didn’t you tell me before that she passed away a long time ago?”
“That’s my eldest sister.”
“You have another sister?”
“Yes.”
“What’s her name?”
“Elaine.”
Daniel waited for her to continue.
Ruth raised her sparse eyebrows.
“I just want to see if you will ask further.”
Claire quickly lowered her head and stuffed sandwiches into her mouth desperately to hide the extremely gloating smile on her lips.
Daniel deserved such a jab.
“I’m sorry.” He said with utmost sincerity.
“I know.”
“No, I don’t think you really understand what I’m apologizing for.”
Ruth slowly put down the tea cup in her hand.

“I apologize for the fact that I have always taken your loyalty to this family for granted as a permanent asset that I bought out in one lump sum many years ago. I apologize for knowing that you were forced to carry the secret that could destroy everyone for Howard, but because I did not want to face the trouble myself, I chose to act deaf and dumb in an extremely selfish way.”
Ruth used her fingers to wrap the string from the tea bag around the handle of the spoon.
“That’s what I willingly chose to bear.”
“I know.”
“So, don’t come here and try to deprive me of my share of guilt after you find out that you are also a coward.”
Daniel nodded silently.
“What about the other employees at the estate?” she asked.
“I don’t know.”
“They’ll be lining up to come to you for letters of recommendation.”
“I’ll write it for them.”
“You have taken the blame and resigned.”
“Even if I leave my job, it won’t affect me from writing a perfect recommendation letter to them.”
“What about your own letters of recommendation?”
Daniel’s eyes drifted to the ugly scorch mark in front of the fireplace.
“I’m going to find someone to write about it who hasn’t seen this fucking kitchen tonight.”
Ruth finally couldn’t hold it back, and a faint smile appeared on her lips.
Claire popped the last crustless piece of the sandwich into her mouth.
At two o’clock in the morning, the mansion at the center of the storm finally fell into complete silence.

Daniel curled up in the sofa chair in the living room for the night in an extremely dejected manner, because he now felt that even climbing the stairs to the second floor was as desperate as climbing Mount Everest. Claire slept in the guest room closest to the stairs. Ruth returned to her room after throwing the sewing basket that contained countless secrets into the trash can in the corridor.
Before dawn, Daniel was awakened by an extremely subtle sound of sweeping the floor.
He saw Ruth kneeling before the fireplace, using a small brush to sweep the last tiny bits of ceramic into a paper bag.
“I thought the police had taken away all the evidence,” he said hoarsely.
“They only took away what they thought would be incriminating.”
“Don’t worry about it.”
“I’ve left too much mess in this house that I can’t clean up.”
Daniel knelt down and silently helped her clean up.
They remained silent in perfect agreement. At the very edge of the bookshelf, he touched a ceramic shard with a picture of a very lonely blue reed. He turned it over in his palm.
“Howard bought this vase in Vermont.” Ruth suddenly said in a confused voice.
“I always thought it was an antique bonus from the old house.”
“Not at all. It was a parallel import that he bought for a huge sum of money in an extremely tacky hotel souvenir shop.”
“Why buy it?”
“Because he was so obsessed with that blue color up there.”
Daniel silently placed the fragment into the paper bag.
“This truth is really disappointing.”
“Not every piece of junk in this world has a great metaphor hidden behind it.”
He glanced up at her.
Ruth ignored him and continued to sweep the floor with great persistence.
When the sun rose, the ground in front of the fireplace had been cleared except for the black scorch mark like a huge scar.
In the weeks that followed, that thrilling night was quickly reduced to a pile of cold legal paperwork, endless interrogation transcripts and nauseating PR calls.

Veronica was formally charged with multiple felonies including unlawful discharge of a hazard flare, making threats of violence, vandalism, and malicious interference with emergency communications systems. The specific wording of the accusations continued to escalate as prosecutors peeled back layers of evidence. Her defense attorney tried to portray her as a victim of a mental breakdown, arguing tearfully in court that she had deliberately avoided everyone in the room and acted out purely due to the severe acute psychological trauma she suffered. But the prosecutor showed a piece of irrefutable evidence in an extremely cold manner: fiber optic cables that were deliberately cut, top-secret documents that were hidden, and the most deadly thing - after she held up a metal candlestick to intimidate two unarmed women, she was still able to calmly take out a loaded flare gun from a locked safe drawer.
Daniel was questioned repeatedly by the police about every minute detail about the amendment and the misappropriated investor funds.

Like an emotionless repeater, he stated everything he knew, what he suspected, and everything he chose, most deliberately, to be deaf to. He voluntarily handed over piles of correspondence, financial audit reports and meeting minutes. Some of the evidence makes him look like a consummate steward with extreme caution, while other evidence makes his so-called “caution” seem extremely mean and deliberate.

In an extremely hypocritical manner, the Board of Directors of the Foundation Trust first announced that he would be suspended with pay to undergo an internal review, and then smoothly approved his resignation that he had already submitted. In their public relations statement, they thanked him for his “outstanding contributions” over the years in a very formal way, without even mentioning a single punctuation mark about the fatal documents that had been deliberately concealed.
Plans to sell the Marlow estate have been put on hold indefinitely.
Investors who had been defrauded of all their hard-earned money were like sharks smelling blood, launching one compensation lawsuit after another.

Howard’s foundation was forced to bring in a so-called “independent” investigation agency to conduct a comprehensive review - although Daniel knew very well that in this circle, the so-called “independence” largely depended on who was paying for this expensive investigation. Several small charities that rely heavily on foundation grants received a cold notice that future funding could face a lengthy freeze. Two junior employees called Daniel in great panic and tentatively asked him if they should quickly prepare to submit their resumes and find a new job. Daniel responded cruelly in the affirmative, and after hanging up the phone, he felt extremely disgusted by his “honesty.”

Ruth went through the extremely cumbersome official procedures and officially handed over the informed consent form to the investigation team as the core physical evidence - even though the document had long been forcibly taken away from the manor by the police. At the same time, she submitted her resignation extremely decisively, announcing that she would leave completely at the end of the month.
## Chapter Sixteen
Claire stayed at the manor for nine more days.

She slept until midnight every day, extremely unusually helped Ruth count the piles of sheets and quilts, and refused to step into Daniel’s office like she was avoiding the plague. Once, Daniel accidentally found her standing at the door like a lost soul, staring blankly at the old photo of Anna.
“Take it away,” he said softly.
“This is your thing.”
“I still have the negatives.”
“That’s not the point.”
He waited quietly.
Claire picked up the old photo frame and very carefully wiped off a fingerprint on the glass with the corner of her clothes.
“My mother hated this photo when she was alive.”
“She thought the photo made her hair look like a ball of dead grass.”
“She said that the reason why you always only choose photos of her smiling heartlessly is because you don’t know how to face those painful moments when she doesn’t smile.”
Daniel slumped against the bookshelf.
“She’s right.”
“Before she died, did she know that you would shamelessly stay in this manor and not leave?”
“We have never discussed this extremely unfortunate topic.”
“You must have discussed it!”

“We discussed, very rationally, whether or not to sell our crappy house. We discussed your college tuition. We discussed whether I should take a long vacation. But we very deliberately avoided the word 'later.'”
“Why?!”
“Because once we start talking about 'the future,' it is a cruel acknowledgment that the world will soon usher in a future without her.”
Claire hugged the frame tightly to the front of her sweater.
“But you ended up being extremely selfish and choosing Howard.”
Daniel’s eyes moved extremely slowly to the top-secret safe hidden behind the biography.
“…Yes.”
She nodded very gently.
There were no hysterical arguments. But this extremely dead silence was more like a Ling Chi’s knife than any vicious curse.

On the last morning of her departure, Daniel drove her to the train station in the manor’s large SUV. They drove along the county road, past the intersection where the emergency vehicle had turned toward the estate that fateful night. No one mentioned it very deliberately.
On the empty platform of the train station, Claire pulled her duffel bag out of the back seat.
“Will you come to Chicago to see me?” she asked suddenly.
“When?”
“I don’t know. Any time will do.”
“That sounds really perfunctory.”
“It’s always a lot more specific than 'Never come.'”
Daniel closed the car door as hard as he could.
“I’ll go.”
“Don’t say something just because you think it’s the perfect politically correct answer.”
“I will go because I am extremely eager to go.”
“You were also extremely eager to stay in the hospital and accompany your mother on her final journey.”
A train made an extremely harsh roar at a distant crossing.

Daniel felt that the extremely familiar defense mechanism established for self-protection was awakening in his body: it was Howard who called me away in an extremely urgent manner; the foundation was facing an extremely fatal audit crisis; it was Anna who extremely generously advised me to deal with it quickly with the overall situation in mind. Every extremely objective fact is true. But put together, it’s still extremely despicable.
“Yes, I did want to stay.” He admitted with great difficulty.
Claire tugged extremely hard on the strap of her duffel bag.
“This is the most despairing thing.”
Before getting in the car, she gave him a very stiff hug.
This hug was extremely short. It by no means represents complete forgiveness, but at least it is no longer some extremely cruel punishment.
Daniel stood on the platform like a stone sculpture until the last car of the train completely disappeared from sight.
Two months later, Veronica wrote him a letter.

The letter was delivered through her defense lawyer in an extremely business-like manner, with not a single word of confession between the lines. She shrewdly offered him a deal: As long as he agreed to sign an out-of-court settlement of her housing claim, she would cooperate and testify in his favor during the Foundation’s full investigation. She shamelessly emphasized in her letter that Howard desperately hoped that she could always maintain some kind of connection with the manor. If she is completely kicked out like garbage now, it will be tantamount to rewarding those extremely hypocritical trust directors who turned a blind eye to Howard’s tyranny and pretending to be deaf and dumb, and extremely cruelly punishing her, a weak woman who was most deceived by Howard and had no power to resist.
Daniel read this extremely ridiculous letter twice.
That day, he didn’t reply a word.

A week later, he calmly agreed to a recorded interview with Veronica’s defense attorney. He described Veronica’s meticulous care of Howard during his deathbed in an extremely objective and unemotional manner. At the same time, he also extremely cold-bloodedly restored the maliciously cut optical cable, the threatening metal candlestick, the deadly flare gun, and all the extremely extreme atrocities she took to steal the amendment and the informed consent form.
Veronica’s lawyer asked Daniel very skillfully whether he really believed deep down in his heart that Veronica had very clear subjective malice and wanted to seriously harm him.
Daniel looked out at the gray sky through the window of the tiny apartment he rented above a shabby Madison pharmacy.

“I am extremely convinced that in order to achieve complete control of those top-secret documents,” he said extremely slowly, “she had fallen into a kind of extreme madness at that time and did not mind dragging all of us into the water.”
“That’s not the question I asked you at all.” The lawyer was furious.
“That’s my final answer.”

This extremely sensational criminal case ended with an out-of-court plea bargain and even a formal trial was skipped. Veronica reluctantly pleaded guilty to misdemeanor charges of illegally firing a flare, malicious damage to property, and intentionally interfering with emergency communications systems. The fatal charge of “intention to cause grievous bodily harm”, which was likely to land her in jail, was eventually withdrawn by the prosecutor due to the lack of extremely conclusive direct evidence. She was sentenced to extremely harsh probation and residential surveillance, sky-high compensation, mandatory and extremely lengthy psychological treatment, and an extremely severe ban - a lifelong ban on direct contact with Claire or Ruth in any way.
Daniel learned these details from extremely cold public court records and extremely brief phone calls with lawyers.
The extremely fierce battle for the trust property dragged on for a long time.

That damn amendment was ultimately reluctantly recognized by the court as some extremely vague evidence of Howard’s lifetime wishes, but it in no way constituted any unconditional transfer of assets. The extremely harsh repayment terms in the informed consent form became an absolutely insurmountable Achilles' heel for Veronica. There was no way she could conjure up the entire two hundred thousand dollars. In the end, like a beggar, the Trust and Estate Committee reached an extremely stingy limited housing subsidy plan with her, which completely sealed her dream of spending the rest of her life in Marlowe Manor.
This extremely mediocre ending failed to truly satisfy anyone.
But Daniel is extremely aware that in this fucked-up world, “no one is satisfied” is often the closest sign to “fairness.”

Although the foundation’s vitality was severely damaged, it managed to survive. An extremely rigorous internal review ultimately concluded that Howard had egregiously misappropriated restricted special funds during his lifetime, and that the entire oversight system around him had long been ineffective and completely rotten. Daniel received an extremely severe internal reprimand for his cowardly concealment of the amendment and his shameful choice to remain deaf when the black hole of investor funds was discovered. But he was not accused in the most absurd way of being an accomplice in enriching his own pockets.
This extremely small difference may make a huge difference in the cold professional resume.
But deep down in his own extremely broken heart, it no longer held any vital significance as he had once so paranoidly believed.

The Marlowe estate was sold to a nonprofit conference center the following spring in an extremely low-key sale. The only good thing is that the buyer graciously agreed to keep the vast majority of the ground floor maintenance staff. The West Wing had been crudely transformed into lifeless offices. The luxurious suite that Veronica had been eager to occupy had been separated into two extremely cramped express suites in an extremely casual manner. The extremely majestic stone fireplace was preserved, along with the extremely ugly black scorch mark on the bottom that could never be erased.
Ruth moved to Pennsylvania.

Daniel worked extremely hard to help her stuff large and small packages into a dilapidated rented truck. The sewing basket, which concealed countless secrets, was donated to charity with great decisiveness. The paperback novels she used to fill her spare time were crammed haphazardly into three cartons ostentatiously labeled “mysteries”—even though one of the boxes was filled with greasy old cookbooks because Ruth had lost her patience with sorting them in the middle of packing.
Before leaving, she handed Daniel an extremely inconspicuous shock-proof bubble envelope in an extremely abrupt manner.
It contained the ceramic shard with a picture of a very lonely blue reed.
“I thought the police had already taken it away as an extremely important exhibit.” He said with great surprise.
“They gave back all the remaining scraps that were extremely useless.”
“Why did you leave it to me?”
“Because I remember very clearly that you were staring at that extremely empty fireplace like a lost fool.”
“That’s hardly an answer at all.”
“Yes,” said Ruth, very calmly, “it really doesn’t count.”
He drove her to the airport.
Outside the extremely crowded terminal, Ruth awkwardly hugged him with one arm, because her other hand was stubbornly clutching her old handbag.
“Remember to say hello to Elaine for me, and ask her where the photo she took on the beach was.” She said extremely abruptly.
“Why?”
“Because I know very well that you have always wanted to know the answer just like Cat Scratch.”
“I do want to know.”
“I understand perfectly.”
She turned around very neatly and walked through the sensor glass door without even looking back.

Daniel threw the extremely ordinary piece of ceramic shards very casually in the drawer of the kitchen of his simple apartment, mixed with a pile of extremely cheap spare batteries and extremely greasy take-out menus. It didn’t deserve to be enshrined in a prominent position on any fireplace. What’s more, the shabby apartment he rented didn’t have any damn fireplace at all.

He found an extremely boring job in an extremely marginal municipal agency, responsible for managing several extremely dilapidated historical buildings. The salary is extremely poor. The office is always filled with an extremely pungent smell of old paper and rust from old radiators. Every extremely minor renovation decision must go through an extremely long and extremely bureaucratic public hearing, written bidding, and an extremely exaggerated dozen-signature approval process.
But he pervertedly enjoyed this excruciating bureaucratic red tape.
Because under extremely transparent rules, any extremely dark secrets will have nowhere to hide.
In June, he went to Chicago to visit Claire.

She shared an extremely shabby apartment with two extremely noisy roommates. Downstairs was an extremely greasy fast food restaurant, and the exhaust fan roared extremely arrogantly all night long. Daniel spent the night curled up in extreme pain on a folding sofa that had collapsed severely in the middle. Claire apologized to him in an extremely perfunctory manner, and then ridiculed him extremely harshly: for the past fifteen years, he had cold-bloodedly preached to all guests at the manor that this extremely uncomfortable experience can temper a person’s extremely strong will.
They had a very humble breakfast at her very rickety little kitchen table.
Claire poured the coffee into an extremely cheap mug with a cracked rim very casually, and pushed it in front of him very rudely.
“You actually came.” She said.
“I most solemnly promised I would come.”
“You’re extremely good at making all kinds of empty promises.”
“I put it on my calendar extremely seriously.”
“This is much more binding on you than swearing on a very sacred Bible.”
He smiled.
She also smiled briefly.

The old photo of Anna smiling brightly and holding a birthday cake was casually pasted on the extremely peeling paint of the refrigerator door with a cheap refrigerator magnet in the shape of a tomato. Claire had long since removed it from the extremely heavy frame.
Daniel stared at it for a long time.
“I thought you hated that picture frame so much that you took it away.”
“I really hate that very vulgar picture frame.”
“That was chosen very carefully by your mother herself.”
“Her taste in picking frames is absolutely disastrous.”
“It’s truly extremely disastrous.”
Claire sat down across from the extremely narrow dining table.
“Do you miss that terribly empty house?”
Daniel considered extremely seriously whether to give an extremely hypocritical but safe negative answer.
“Occasionally.”
“What part of it do you desperately miss?”

“The extremely quiet morning before everyone wakes up. The extremely dull thud of those extremely old heating pipes. And the extremely clear knowledge of which key in my pocket will open which door with extremely precise precision.”
“This sounds very much like the confessions of an extremely perverted control freak.”
“Most likely yes.”
“Is there anything else?”

He looked through the extremely dirty window glass at the mottled exterior wall of the extremely depressing red brick building next door. Someone placed a broken box-type electric fan on the fire escape in an extremely illegal and extremely dangerous manner. An extremely plump pigeon stood beside it very leisurely, enjoying the extremely weak warm wind blowing its extremely dirty feathers.
“I miss Ruth so much every Monday she would break down and complain about the flowers that arrived.”
“She actually complained about flowers?”

“Every Monday, unshakable. She complained extremely viciously about the extremely hypocritical rich people who pervertedly asked the florist to spend a full forty minutes to carefully arrange a pot of flower arrangements that looked extremely 'casual' and extremely 'original'.”
Claire was extremely bored and tore off the cardboard cover from the coffee cup and folded it into an extremely long and thin strip.
“So you miss Howard terribly?”

Daniel quickly recalled the extremely secret brass moisture-proof cylinder, the extremely crucial missing page, the extremely life-saving treatment fee, the extremely expensive bottle of decanter in the library, and the extremely contradictory man who pulled him out extremely selfishly, but also treated him extremely cold-bloodedly as an extremely useful tool.
“Yes.” He said with utmost candor.
“Have you been extremely forgiving of him?”
“No.”
Claire nodded with great understanding.
“Then are you extremely forgiving of Veronica?”
“No.”
Another extremely calm nod.
“Then you...are you extremely forgiving of yourself?”
Daniel looked at her in great astonishment.
She asked the question in an extremely matter-of-fact tone, neither with the most false comfort nor with the most unkind accusation.
“It’s extremely difficult and can’t be done at once.” He said extremely dryly.
Claire pressed the folded paper flatly on the table with great force.
“That sounds extremely maddening.”
“Extremely crazy.”
They drank the rest of their coffee in perfect silence.
Before Daniel was extremely ready to leave, Claire handed him an extremely small envelope extremely abruptly.

Inside was an extremely crude photo that she printed out very casually on her phone. That was the scene in the living room of Marlowe Manor a few days after the flare gun incident. The extremely glaring broken vase had been cleaned up extremely thoroughly. The carpet, which was burned beyond recognition, was also dug up with great violence. The extremely pale morning light swept across the extremely bare floor very coldly, and finally stayed extremely weakly on the extremely ugly blackened mark next to the fireplace.
In the photo, it is extremely deserted.
“I took this very deliberately photo of that extremely sinful house before it was completely sold,” she said.
“Why?”
“I just want to remember in a very profound way how tragic it really was after all the crazy stuff has settled.”
Daniel stared at the photo with great concentration.

Not during Howard’s extremely authoritarian reign. Not before Veronica came back with great arrogance. Not before Daniel told that big lie, so incredibly hypocritically. It was after an extremely complete collapse.
He put it away in the inner pocket of his suit with the utmost solemnity.

In the extremely noisy train station, Claire stood with him extremely patiently until the radio announced his train number in an extremely harsh tone. They stood extremely cramped under the extremely large and extremely cold electronic stop sign. The extremely numb people around them were dragging extremely heavy suitcases in an extremely hurry, carrying extremely cheap coffee, holding extremely vulgar flowers, dragging extremely tired and crying children, and they were flowing past them in an extremely indifferent manner.
“I have one final, very pointed question.” She said suddenly and with great seriousness.
“Ask.”
“That night, when you rushed into the kitchen so heroically, did you know very clearly that the flare was actually aimed at that damn vase?”
“I don’t know.”
“You were so sure that she was going to murder you?”
“Yes.”
“But you still stood in front of us extremely instinctively.”
Daniel looked at her with great confusion.
“I don’t remember any great decisions I made in my head at the time.”
“That’s not a question I asked you at all.”

He understood very deeply that she was not asking him superficially whether he was an extremely fearless hero at that time. She was desperately searching, after stripping away those extremely disgusting lies, extremely hypocritical excuses, and the extremely stupid fifteen years he had squandered in this extremely cursed house, whether his body could still make an instinctive action that she could trust with utmost honesty and without reservation.
“Yes,” he said hoarsely, “I blocked you very instinctively.”
Claire’s eyes were extremely red for a moment, but she held back the tears with great force.
“Okay.”
The train door slid open with an icy coldness.
Daniel stepped onto the carriage very heavily, and turned around very quickly before the extremely crowded crowd separated them cruelly.
Claire was still standing extremely lonely on the extremely empty platform. Very slowly she raised a hand.
He also raised his hand extremely slowly.
The car door closed with the utmost ruthlessness.

As the train pulled away with great heaviness, Daniel took the photo out of his pocket with extreme caution. The extremely charred fireplace base captured the extremely bleak morning light in an extremely dazzling way. That extremely empty room looked neither extremely redeemed nor extremely completely destroyed. It only presents an extremely tired appearance that is extremely real, has been extremely roughly used, has been extremely ruthlessly changed, and extremely honestly exposes its true appearance of being extremely cruelly devoured by extremely violent flames.

He held the photo very tightly until the very familiar station completely disappeared from the extremely blurred vision, and then, very solemnly, he hid it very deeply in his bag together with the piece of ceramic fragment with the very lonely blue reed painted on it.
zh: ## 第一章
她发际线处的抓痕已经停止了渗血，一条细微的红线隐没在褐色的发丝间。
“是我带她来的。” 克莱尔（Claire）打破了僵局。
丹尼尔（Daniel）紧扣着维罗妮卡（Veronica）手腕的手指，力道微微松了一分。
露丝（Ruth）错愕地盯着她。
维罗妮卡微微侧过身，越过自己的肩膀看向丹尼尔。她脸上的表情变化极其细微，甚至透出一丝令人毛骨悚然的柔和。
“你真的什么都不知道，对吧？”
丹尼尔空出一只手，一把拉开中岛台旁的一把吧台椅。
“坐下。”
维罗妮卡瞥了一眼椅子。
“我叫你坐下。”
她顺从了。丹尼尔依然死死钳住她的一只手腕，同时，露丝拿起了那把信号枪，像拿着个烫手山芋似的，伸直了手臂把它放到了最远处的流理台上。
“把它打开。” 丹尼尔命令道。
露丝惶恐地看着他。
“那把信号枪。检查里面是不是空的。”
“我……我不知道怎么弄。”
“扳机护环旁边有个释放钮。”
她的双手抖得太厉害，信号枪在大理石台面上磕出刺耳的脆响。克莱尔走过去，把它从露丝手里接了过来。
“给我吧。” 丹尼尔沉声说。
“我知道怎么操作。” 克莱尔回了一句。
“你怎么知道的？”
克莱尔按下释放钮，枪管应声弹开，里面露出一枚已经击发的铝制弹壳。
丹尼尔看着她。
“湖区安全课程，” 她解释道，“当初是你非逼着我上了两次。”
露丝穿过厨房，拿起挂在食品储藏室门旁的无绳电话。她按下通话键，听了一会儿。
“没有盲音，线断了。”
“昨天的暴风雨把外线刮断了。” 丹尼尔说，“用我的手机打。”
“你的手机在客厅里。” 克莱尔接话。
“你怎么知道？”
“我刚才看到了。”
丹尼尔的视线越过她。他的手机正静静地躺在浅色地毯的边缘，屏幕一片漆黑。
“去拿过来。” 他对露丝说。
维罗妮卡笔直地坐在吧台椅上，一只手腕依然在丹尼尔的掌控之中。她没有挣扎。绸缎袖子滑落了一截，露出小臂上的一块淤青。丹尼尔不记得自己弄伤过她，但还是下意识地放松了手劲。
露丝拿着手机回来了。
“屏幕碎了。”
“之前就碎了。”
“怎么按都亮不了。”
丹尼尔接过来，按下侧边键，又把它在掌心磕了两下。毫无反应。
“用克莱尔的手机。” 他说。
克莱尔低头盯着地板。
“手机在哪？”
“在你的办公室里。”
“它在我的办公室里干什么？”
维罗妮卡嘴角勾起一抹极淡的冷笑。
直到这一刻，丹尼尔才真正摸清了今晚这场闹剧的轮廓。
他的目光从克莱尔身上移开，落在了那个碎裂的花瓶上。那不过是个普通的白色陶瓷花瓶，手工绘制着细长的蓝色芦苇。它在壁炉旁摆了好些年了。即便在霍华德·韦尔（Howard Vale）死后，这座房子变得不再像个家，而更像是一具等待解剖的昂贵尸体，露丝依然坚持每个星期一为它换上鲜花。
而在那些陶瓷碎片之间，躺着一个比地毯颜色更深的东西。
一张边缘被严重烧焦的厚羊皮纸。
维罗妮卡注意到他的视线定格了。
丹尼尔松开了她的手腕。
他大步走到壁炉前，蹲下身。石板上依然散发着余温。信号弹在壁炉地面上凿出了一个焦黑的深坑，甚至融化了一小块地毯。他用两根手指小心翼翼地捏起那张残纸。
纸上只有三个词还勉强能认出来。
信托修正案。
他站起身。
克莱尔微微扬起下巴，尽管她的脸色已经苍白如纸。
丹尼尔举起那块烧焦的残片。
“你到底从我的办公室里拿走了什么？”
无人应答。
“克莱尔。”
她的大拇指死死地搓着毛衣的接缝。
“我上周就发现了。”
“发现什么？”
“你心知肚明。”
“我要听你亲口说出来。”
“霍华德的修正案。”
露丝喉咙里发出一声低呼，颓然跌坐在最近的吧台椅上。
丹尼尔死死盯着她。她躲开了他的视线。
维罗妮卡将双手平放在膝盖上。她似乎又恢复了那种高高在上的镇定，但丹尼尔看穿了她强撑的伪装——她的手指太过用力地抓着绸缎布料，胸口的起伏也显得短促而吃力。
“你当初信誓旦旦地告诉我，这东西根本不存在。” 她冷冷地说。
丹尼尔依然盯着露丝。
“霍华德死后，我直截了当地问过你。你站在图书馆里，看着我的眼睛告诉我，绝对没有任何后续的文件。”
“绝对没有任何‘具备法律效力’的后续文件。” 丹尼尔反驳。
“你当时的原话可不是这么说的。”
“他在签那份东西的时候，已经病得神志不清了！”
“他签字的时候确实快死了，但这和‘神志不清’是两码事。”
克莱尔朝壁炉挪近了一步。丹尼尔下意识地挡在了那张烧焦的残纸前。
“你翻了我的文件柜。” 丹尼尔质问女儿。
“是你把它藏起来了。”
“那间办公室是上了锁的！”
“我知道你把备用钥匙藏在哪儿。”
“你当然知道。”
这句话脱口而出时带着一股浓烈的讥讽，连他们父女俩自己都被刺痛了。
克莱尔瞪着他：“你这话是什么意思？”
“意思是，你一直把这座房子当成一个游乐场，所有的规矩对别人适用，唯独对你例外。”
“这可是我从你身上学到的。”
露丝痛苦地闭上了眼睛。
维罗妮卡嘴角的冷笑消失了。房间里的空气仿佛凝固了。透过巨大的落地窗，傍晚的余晖在马罗湖（Marrow Lake）上铺开一道道狭长的银色光带。一艘摩托艇在对岸驶过，距离太远了，船上的人根本不可能知道，这座显赫的韦尔庄园里，刚刚有人在室内发射了一枚致命的信号弹。
丹尼尔把那块残纸对折了一下。
“剩下的部分在哪？”
“被信号弹烧成了灰。” 维罗妮卡说。
克莱尔摇了摇头。
丹尼尔转向她。
“原件根本不在那个花瓶里。” 她说。
维罗妮卡猛地站了起来，吧台椅的腿在地板上刮出刺耳的噪音。
丹尼尔立刻挡在她们中间。
“坐下。”
“她骗了我！” 维罗妮卡尖叫。
“所以你就拿信号枪指着她？！”
“我瞄准的是花瓶！”
“你在一间屋子里开了枪！旁边十英尺不到的地方就站着三个活人！”
“是她告诉我文件就藏在里面的！”
“所以你觉得一把火烧了它是最理智的应对方式？”
“我没想烧了它！”
丹尼尔指着焦黑的壁炉底座。
“那你到底想干什么？”
维罗妮卡张了张嘴，却卡壳了。
克莱尔替她回答了。
“她以为文件被密封在花瓶的夹层里了。”
露丝愕然地看向那堆碎片：“密封？”
“她认定霍华德把签好字的副本封死在里面了。”
“他为什么要干这种荒唐事？”
“因为维罗妮卡告诉我，霍华德生前一直在防着我爸，偷偷藏东西。”
丹尼尔猛地转向维罗妮卡。
“你到底都在跟她胡说八道些什么？”
“主要是实话。”
“主要是。” 丹尼尔咀嚼着这个词。
“我告诉她，霍华德早就对你失去了信任。”
“霍华德在觉得自己是个大善人的时候，信任全世界；在觉得自己是个聪明人的时候，谁都不信。这一点，你比任何人都清楚。”
## 第二章
维罗妮卡的脸孔绷紧了。
丹尼尔心想，终于露馅了。她不是疯了，至少目前还没疯。这是一种带着明确目的的恶意。
维罗妮卡是在霍华德去世前三年搬进马罗庄园的。起初，她只是东翼慈善基金会的一名顾问；后来，她成了一个所有人都心照不宣、却绝口不提的“女伴”。她会穿着丝绸晚礼服出席高规格晚宴，也会光着脚在早餐桌上批阅拨款提案。七十一岁、刚刚丧偶的霍华德固执地向佣人们宣布，他们的私人关系与庄园的运作无关。
维罗妮卡也一直配合着这种表演，直到这种关系与“遗嘱”扯上关系为止。
丹尼尔在有确切理由之前，就已经对她心生反感。现在他敢私下承认这一点了。她侵占这栋房子空间的速度太快了。她不打招呼就开他珍藏的红酒，按照自己那套诡异的逻辑把书架上的书挪来挪去。她当着员工的面亲昵地叫霍华德“H”。她跟丹尼尔说话的语气，仿佛他这十五年来为庄园呕心沥血的管理，不过是一场冗长的行政失误。
后来，霍华德病倒了，而维罗妮卡留了下来。
她熟记了他所有的药单，整夜整夜地睡在他床边的陪护椅上，在电话里跟护士据理力争。当丹尼尔连一口水都喂不进去时，她总有办法哄着霍华德吃下半片吐司。不管她骨子里到底是个什么样的人，在那段最难熬的日子里，她从未缺席。
这让丹尼尔此刻捏在手里的残纸，变得犹如千斤重。
“我要拿克莱尔的手机。” 他深吸了一口气。
“在你办公桌最下面的抽屉里。” 维罗妮卡冷冷地说。
丹尼尔没有看她：“为什么在那儿？”
“为了防止她打电话给你求救。”
克莱尔的声音平淡如水：“是我自己放进去的。”
“为什么？”
“因为我太了解你了，你肯定会把今晚的一切搞成一场‘英雄救女’的戏码。”
“你当时正躲在中岛台后面，而有人正举着沉重的烛台要砸向你！”
“她没拿那个打我。”
“她抓伤了你！”
“那是我自己撞在橱柜把手上划伤的。”
露丝看了一眼克莱尔发际线上的伤。
“当 Hale 小姐举起烛台的时候，我一把拽倒了克莱尔，” 管家作证道，“她撞到了抽屉把手。”
丹尼尔立刻把矛头转向露丝：“今天早上我从密尔沃基打电话回来的时候，你明明告诉我家里一切太平！”
“我当时说，那一刻确实很安静。”
丹尼尔忍不住发出一声极其难听的冷笑。
维罗妮卡在一旁冷眼旁观。“这就是这座房子的特色，不是吗？每一句回答，从字面上看都是毫无破绽的真理。”
丹尼尔走到流理台前，拿起那把信号枪。枪管依然敞开着，铝制弹壳清晰可见。他合上枪管，把它塞进冰箱上方的吊柜里，然后拔下了柜门的钥匙。
“露丝，你看着她。”
露丝的眉毛挑了起来。
“看着我？” 维罗妮卡觉得有些可笑。
“露丝，如果她试图靠近任何抽屉、大门、重物，或者任何能点燃的东西，立刻告诉我。”
“那我告诉您之后，我该干什么？”
“什么都不用干。”
“终于，” 维罗妮卡讥讽道，“一个配得上大管家身份的完美计划。”
丹尼尔没搭理她。
他走进客厅去拿自己的手机，尽管他心里清楚这东西已经成了一块废铁。屏幕的一角彻底碎裂了。他死死按住电源键，屏幕上闪过一道微弱的绿线，随即又陷入死寂。旁边地毯上扔着他的过夜旅行袋，拉链都没拉。这是他刚才听到尖叫声时，随手扔下的。
他身后的玻璃门大敞着。
透过门，他能把厨房里的景象尽收眼底：克莱尔站在壁炉旁，露丝局促地坐在凳子上，维罗妮卡重新坐好，双手老老实实地放在明处。这画面，简直像是一张没人愿意按快门的诡异全家福。
丹尼尔拎起旅行袋，走到玄关的控制台前。他的笔记本电脑在里面。他打开电脑，按下电源键，屏幕亮了起来。
无线网络显示：无连接。
“路由器罢工了。” 他喊道。
无人回应。
他把笔记本端回了厨房。
“安保面板有蜂窝网络备用系统，” 他一边走一边说，“我可以从那里发送紧急求救信号。”
“它刚才一直在闪红灯。” 露丝提醒道。
“在哪儿？”
“在设备走廊。”
丹尼尔快步穿过厨房。洗衣房旁边的安保面板果然闪烁着刺眼的红光。系统故障。蜂窝模块离线。
他输入了维修代码。故障日志显示，在今天下午 3:12 分，外部信号彻底丢失。
他蹲下身，检查了下面柜子里的调制解调器。电源线被拔掉了。
丹尼尔死死盯着那个插头。
克莱尔出现在走廊尽头。
“不是我拔的。”
“我还没问你。”
“你的眼神已经问了。”
“回厨房去。”
“回去！”
她执拗地站在原地。
设备走廊很窄，墙上挂满了这座房子在霍华德翻新之前的老照片。其中一张拍于五十年代，那时的厨房还是深色木质橱柜和油毡地板。几个卷起袖子的男人站在现在大理石中岛台的位置。照片里的每个人，看起来都不怎么情愿被拍。
丹尼尔把调制解调器的插头重新插上。面板上的指示灯开始跳动。
“是维罗妮卡拔的吗？” 克莱尔问。
“我不知道。”
“肯定是她。”
“你怎么知道？”
“我亲眼看到她从这儿走出去的。”
“在你藏起手机之前，还是之后？”
克莱尔的嘴唇抿成了一条直线。
丹尼尔等着路由器重新连接。毫无动静。他拆开最底下的检修面板，赫然发现外部的主光缆被人齐刷刷地剪断了。
他回头看着女儿。
“你看到她拿刀了吗？”
“没有。”
“剪刀呢？”
“没有。”
“那你什么都不知道。”
“你现在居然在替她辩护？！”
“我是在试图搞清楚到底发生了什么该死的事！”
“你大可以心平气和地问我！”
“从我踏进厨房的那一秒起，我就一直在问你！”
“你那叫审问！”
丹尼尔猛地摔上了设备柜的门，声音震耳欲聋。
克莱尔吓得缩了一下肩膀。
这个退缩的动作持续了不到一秒钟，她恢复得如此之快，如果丹尼尔不是她父亲，可能根本察觉不到。
他强压下怒火，放低了声音。
“从头开始说。”
她警惕地瞥了一眼厨房的方向。“别当着她的面。”
“也别当着露丝的面。”
这个要求本身，就已经泄露了太多的信息。
丹尼尔望向厨房。露丝僵硬地坐着，双手交叠在腿上。维罗妮卡则像一头警觉的猎豹一样盯着走廊，她显然已经意识到，有些见不得光的秘密正在避开她悄然运作。
“去客厅。” 丹尼尔下令。
他率先走了过去，把是否跟上来的选择权留给了克莱尔。
## 第三章
她还是跟了过来。
丹尼尔关上了一扇玻璃门，但刻意留了另一扇微敞着，以确保能听到厨房里的动静。房子里静得可怕。连冰箱的压缩机似乎都停止了嗡嗡声。
克莱尔没有坐沙发，而是局促地坐在了一张扶手椅的边缘。
“霍华德的信托修正案，真的是你故意藏起来的吗？” 她开门见山。
丹尼尔把那块成了废铁的手机扔在咖啡桌上。
“这不该是故事的开头。”
“对我来说，这就是。”
“克莱尔。”
“你只需要回答是，或者不是。”
他看着她额头上的抓痕，重重地吐出一个字：“是。”
她茫然地眨了眨眼。
他原本以为会迎来一场暴怒的控诉，或者是某种揭穿他真面目的得意。然而，她脸上浮现的，只有一种透支了的、远超她年龄的疲惫和失望。
“你一直骗我说她在撒谎。”
“我当时说的是，她对这座庄园没有任何‘可执行的’法定所有权。”
“这根本就是在玩文字游戏。”
“是的。”
“妈妈知道这事吗？”
“不知道。”
克莱尔转过头，望向窗外的湖面。
太阳已经躲进了一层厚厚的云层后面，抽走了湖面波光粼粼的光泽。客厅里依然明亮，但天花板边缘的阴影已经开始不可阻挡地加深。
丹尼尔在她的对面坐下。
“在霍华德去世前十一天，他签署了一份拟议的修正案。条款赋予了维罗妮卡对西翼建筑的终身使用权，一笔由基金会按年支付的年金，以及如果庄园未来被出售，她将获得一定比例的变现分成。”
“百分之多少？”
“百分之十五。”
“但她告诉我的是百分之二十。”
“在我看到的那份文件上，是百分之十五。”
“你为什么不把这份文件移交给律师团队？”
“因为霍华德的主治医生当时已经明确提出质疑，认为他是否还具备做出重大财务决策的认知能力。”
“他被认定为无行为能力了吗？”
“医生并没有下最后结论。”
“那你凭什么扣下文件？”
“因为在签署这份文件的两天前，霍华德勃然大怒，指控露丝偷了他的古董袖扣！而那副袖扣，他早在十年前就送给他的亲侄子了！”
“他只是老了，健忘而已。”
“他不仅健忘，他的情绪每小时都在剧烈波动！他把同一幅名画许诺给了三个人！他甚至企图把湖边的船屋过户给一个仅仅来清理过一次排水沟的工人！”
“所以你就越俎代庖，替他决定哪些遗愿算数，哪些作废？”
“我只是把文件暂时封存，直到我们能通过法律手段确认它的有效性为止。”
“你封存了多久？”
丹尼尔沉默了。
克莱尔缓缓地点了点头。“整整六个月。”
“我承认，我本该走程序的。”
“你把它放碎纸机里了？”
“没有。”
“那它在哪？”
“在我办公室的防火保险箱里。”
克莱尔用力搓了搓双手。
“那我拿走的那个到底是什么？”
“一份复印件。”
“你早就知道我拿了？”
“上周我就发现那个文件夹被人动过了。”
“但你连一句都没问过我。”
“我当时以为是露丝进去过。”
克莱尔给了他一个极度荒谬的眼神。
“你当然会这么以为。”
“什么意思？”
“意思是，在你眼里，你永远会优先去怀疑那个拿工资办事的下属，而不是你声称你爱的人。”
丹尼尔差点脱口而出，告诉她“爱”只会让怀疑的代价变得更昂贵，而不是更廉价。但他硬生生把这句话咽了回去，因为这听起来太像霍华德在喝了两杯红酒后会发表的伪善说教了。
“你为什么要联系维罗妮卡？”
“是她先联系我的。”
“怎么联系的？”
“发邮件。”
“她怎么会有你的邮箱？”
“随便找找就有了，这又不难。”
“她在邮件里说了什么？”
“她说霍华德签了一份被你暗中扣押的文件。她甚至附上了一张签名页的照片。”
丹尼尔猛地倾身向前。“给我看那张照片。”
“我的手机在你的办公室里。”
“所以，是在她联系你之后，你才去翻了我的文件柜？”
“然后你引狼入室，把她招到了家里？！”
“她本来就住在这里！”
“她昨天就该搬走了！”
“但她今天下午又回来了。”
“是谁放她进来的？”
克莱尔低下了头。
丹尼尔痛苦地闭上了眼睛。
“你把大门的密码给了她。”
“我以为我们能坐下来把话说清楚。”
“跟一个隐瞒了绝密法律文件的人把话说清楚？”
“是跟你把话说清楚！”
“你指望她能告诉你什么你还不知道的惊天秘密？”
“我指望她能告诉我，你为什么这么怕她。”
“我根本不怕她。”
“你本该怕的。”
丹尼尔转头看向厨房。
维罗妮卡依然端坐在那里。露丝从抽屉里拿出了一条擦碗巾，正把它叠成越来越小的方块。
“是维罗妮卡剪断了网线吗？”
“是的。”
“你刚才还说你没看到她手里拿东西。”
“我确实没看到。是她亲口告诉我，她剪了线。”
“什么时候说的？”
“在露丝把我们在你办公室里抓了个现行之后。”
“你们当时在办公室里干什么？”
“找原件。”
“找到了吗？”
克莱尔摇摇头。
“那她为什么会坚信原件在那个花瓶里？”
“因为是我告诉她的。”
“你疯了吗？为什么？”
“因为她当时手里正攥着那个沉甸甸的黄铜烛台！”
丹尼尔猛地站起身，走到窗前，把手掌重重地贴在冰冷的玻璃上。
“把事情的经过，原原本本、一字不落地告诉我。”
克莱尔一开始说得很慢。
维罗妮卡是在三点刚过的时候到的。她甚至还穿着昨晚参加慈善晚宴的那套高定礼服。她声称酒店的预订到期了，而丹尼尔又冷血地扣留了她还在西翼的两个行李箱。克莱尔信了，放她进了大门。当时露丝正在楼上换床单。
但维罗妮卡根本没有去拿什么行李箱。
她直奔丹尼尔的办公室。
克莱尔紧紧地跟了过去，因为把她放进来本来就是为了摊牌。克莱尔熟练地用那把藏在玄关桌暗格底部的黄铜钥匙开了门。维罗妮卡显然也知道这把钥匙的存在，那是霍华德生前告诉她的。
在办公室里，克莱尔用丹尼尔那串贴着标签的备用钥匙串，打开了锁着的文件柜。她准确地找到了上周曾看到过修正案副本的那个文件夹。
里面空空如也。
维罗妮卡立刻翻脸，指控克莱尔是丹尼尔派来的内鬼，故意打草惊蛇。克莱尔反唇相讥，痛斥维罗妮卡在霍华德生病期间利用他的神志不清进行洗脑。两人的争吵一直压着声音，直到露丝突然推门进来，看到了大敞着的文件柜。
露丝厉声命令维罗妮卡滚出去。
维罗妮卡拒绝。
露丝伸手去拿办公桌上的电话。维罗妮卡一把扯断了电话线，然后冲进设备走廊，用丹尼尔桌上的剪刀直接铰断了主光缆。
“她在搞破坏的时候，你为什么不趁机跑出去？” 丹尼尔怒不可遏。
“我要的是真相。”
“你已经看到真相了！那个文件夹是空的！”
“我要亲耳听到她承认！”
“听露丝承认什么？”
“承认是她伙同你一起藏匿了修正案！”
丹尼尔猛地从窗边转过身。
克莱尔死死地盯着他。
“是她干的吗？” 她逼问。
“我不知道你在说什么。”
“你脸上那副表情已经出卖你了。”
“我只知道，露丝清楚霍华德在临终前签过一些乱七八糟的文件。”
“这根本不是我问你的问题。”
## 第四章
“不是。” 丹尼尔斩钉截铁地回答。
“她没有帮你藏匿文件？”
“没有。”
回答得太快了，连掩饰的时间都没有。
克莱尔站起身。
“你又来了。”
“又来什么？”
“又在用那种‘字面正确’的缩水版真相敷衍我。”
厨房里传来椅子摩擦地板的声音。
维罗妮卡拔高了音量，声音穿透了玻璃门：“问问他那张‘见证人签名页’是怎么回事！”
丹尼尔的胃部猛地一阵痉挛。
克莱尔疑惑地看向微敞的玻璃门。
“什么见证人签名页？”
“待在这儿别动。” 丹尼尔命令道。
维罗妮卡发出一串轻柔而嘲弄的笑声。
露丝似乎低声反驳了一句，声音太小，听不真切。
克莱尔没有听话，径直走进了厨房。丹尼尔紧随其后。
维罗妮卡依然坐在吧台椅上，但身体已经完全转向了露丝的方向。
“你到底干了什么好事？” 克莱尔质问管家。
露丝把那块叠好的擦碗巾放在台面上。它已经被折成了一个比手掌还小的、极其工整的蓝白相间的方块。
“Hale 小姐只是在虚张声势，想吓唬你。”
“霍华德签署修正案的时候，你就在场。”
“是的。”
“你做见证人了吗？”
露丝的目光闪躲着，飘向了丹尼尔。
维罗妮卡像秃鹫一样精准地捕捉到了这个眼神。
“看啊，” 她冷笑着说，“就这一个眼神，已经把这座房子里肮脏的利益同盟暴露无遗了。”
丹尼尔靠在中岛台上，死死地双臂交叉在胸前，试图掩饰手部不受控制的轻微颤抖。
“告诉她，露丝。”
露丝充满戒备地打量着他：“告诉她哪一部分？”
“她问的那一部分。”
露丝一把将那块叠好的毛巾推远。
“霍华德确实要求我在文件上签字作见证。但我拒绝了。”
“为什么？” 克莱尔追问。
“那天早上，他的脑子已经彻底糊涂了。”
“怎么糊涂了？”
“他拉着我的手，叫我 Miriam。”
“Miriam 是谁？”
“他的第一任妻子。”
维罗妮卡的声音瞬间变得尖锐无比：“他很快就纠正过来了！”
“那是在我大声提醒他之后。”
“他清清楚楚地知道自己在签什么！”
“你无权替他断言！”
“在你端着水杯进来之前，我已经陪他聊了整整两个小时！”
“而我，已经陪了他整整二十六年！”
“你不过是个打扫卫生的佣人！”
露丝的脸色变了。
丹尼尔曾无数次亲眼目睹露丝如何不动声色地应付那些把她当成隐形人的傲慢宾客，也见过她如何优雅地回应那些连她名字都记不住、却虚伪地嘘寒问暖的信托董事。她从未流露过半点愠色。但此刻，她看着维罗妮卡的眼神，竟然透出一种令人背脊发凉的平静。
“是啊，” 露丝冷冷地说，“我负责清理你们这些光鲜亮丽的寄生虫留下的所有烂摊子。”
维罗妮卡居然第一个移开了视线，避其锋芒。
克莱尔的目光在两人之间来回扫视。
“如果露丝没有签字作证，那是谁签的？”
“基金会的两个基层员工，” 丹尼尔回答，“他们签了字。”
“那她为什么口口声声提到什么缺失的‘见证人签名页’？”
维罗妮卡抢白道：
“因为霍华德死后，那份签好字的修正案，离奇地缺了最后一页！”
克莱尔眉头紧锁。“但我看到的那份复印件上是有签名的。”
“你看到的，是一份被人动过手脚的拼接扫描件，” 维罗妮卡冷笑，“最初的原始文件明明有十二页，但交到丹尼尔手里的那份原件，只有十一页。”
丹尼尔觉得整个厨房的空间都在向他挤压。
克莱尔震惊地转向他。“这是真的吗？”
“最后一页去哪了？”
“没人知道。”
露丝猛地站了起来。
虽然她的动作依然刻意保持着迟缓和谨慎，但丹尼尔清清楚楚地看到了她眼底重新翻涌起的恐惧。
“霍华德晚年就喜欢干这种把文件拆得七零八落的事，” 她结结巴巴地辩解，“他会在各种文件背面随手记笔记，然后拿着它们在各个房间里乱晃。”
维罗妮卡死死地盯着她。
“你当时可是亲口告诉丹尼尔，那一页已经被销毁了。”
露丝仿佛失去了听觉，一言不发。
丹尼尔放下了交叉的双臂。
“她什么时候告诉过我这种话？”
“就在霍华德去世后的第二天早上。”
“那天早上我几乎寸步不离地跟她在一起处理后事！”
“但你没有跟她一起待在洗衣房里。”
露丝转身朝储藏室走去。丹尼尔大步迈出，挡死了她的去路。
“露丝。”
“我需要喝点水。”
“我去给你倒。”
“我还没残废到倒不了一杯水！”
她的声音虽然极力保持平稳，但她的左手已经控制不住地再次剧烈颤抖起来。
丹尼尔从橱柜里拿出一个玻璃杯，接满了水递给她。露丝一把接过，连句谢谢都没说。她猛灌了半杯，然后把杯子紧紧地贴在羊毛开衫上，仿佛在汲取某种力量。
克莱尔紧追不放：“是你销毁了最后一页吗？”
“没有。”
“那霍华德签完字之后，你见过那一页吗？”
露丝死死盯着杯子里的水面。
维罗妮卡蹭地站了起来。
丹尼尔厉声指着凳子：“坐下！”
“休想！”
“我叫你坐下！”
“你的信号枪里已经没子弹了！”
“我命令你坐下和那把见鬼的枪没关系！”
“在你眼里，今晚的所有事情都只和那把该死的信号枪有关！因为只有死死咬住这一点，才能让你那虚伪的良心觉得你是个无可指责的无辜受害者！”
丹尼尔怒不可遏地逼近一步。
克莱尔敏捷地插进了他们中间。
但她并没有像丹尼尔护着流理台那样，完全挡在维罗妮卡身前。她找了一个极其刁钻的角度，确保能同时把他们两人都纳入视线。
“所有人都待在原地别动。” 她命令道。
丹尼尔难以置信地看着女儿。
她的声音不大，但正因如此，那种不容置疑的威严反而让人难以抗拒。
露丝颓然坐回了凳子上。维罗妮卡依然站着，但并没有再往前迈出一步。
克莱尔指着那块烧焦的地毯。
“她之所以开枪，是因为我骗她，见证人签名页就藏在那个花瓶里。”
丹尼尔瞪大了眼睛。
“你早就知道缺失了一页？！”
“我只知道维罗妮卡在发了疯一样地找它。”
“这根本不是一回事！”
“我看到了她发给你的邮件。”
“在我的私人邮箱里？”
“打印出来压在你的办公桌垫下面。”
丹尼尔瞬间想起来了。三个月前，维罗妮卡在一封措辞极其激烈的邮件中声称，霍华德那份完整的修正案里，包含了一份经过公证的附加声明，该声明详细确认了他的认知能力和真实意图。她愤怒地指控是丹尼尔暗中销毁了那份声明。丹尼尔之所以把它打印出来，是因为纸质的文件能让他从心理上拉开一点距离，显得不那么咄咄逼人。他从未回复过那封邮件。
“我根本不知道那一页到底存不存在，” 克莱尔继续解释，“当她举起烛台的时候，情急之下，我随口胡诌说露丝把它封死在那个花瓶里了。我以为她会像个疯子一样冲过去找。”
“结果她转头去拿了一把信号枪。”
“是的。”
“为什么？！”
维罗妮卡的目光直勾勾地落在那些稀碎的陶瓷片上。
“因为那个花瓶的瓶颈是完全封死的。”
露丝手里的玻璃杯一滑，冰水顺着她的裙子浇了下去。
丹尼尔顺着维罗妮卡的视线看去。
那个花瓶一直是个华而不实的摆设。露丝每次插花时，都是把花插在一个刚好能卡在瓶口里的窄玻璃细管里。花瓶的肚子明明是中空的，但除非你把它砸得粉碎，否则根本不可能把任何东西塞进去。
“你真的以为那份绝密文件在里面。” 丹尼尔倒吸了一口凉气。
“克莱尔言之凿凿地说露丝把它封在里面了。”
“那你为什么不直接把它摔碎？”
“它太重了。”
“它顶多只有六磅重！”
“我当时脑子一片混乱！”
“不，” 丹尼尔咬牙切齿地说，“你当时的脑子清醒得很。你条理清晰地切断了通讯光缆。你瘫痪了安保备用系统。你收缴了克莱尔的手机。你拉开了专门用来上锁的安全抽屉。你熟练地装填了一把信号枪——”
“枪里本来就有子弹。”
“——然后在一间塞满了活人的屋子里，毫无顾忌地开了火！”
“我刻意避开了你们！”
“那颗该死的火球离我的脑袋只有不到三英尺！”
“因为我笃定你一定会躲开。”
## 第五章
丹尼尔死死地盯着她。
她脸上那种理所当然的神情，不仅没有让这句辩解变得合情合理，反而让它显得更加丧心病狂。
“你笃定我会躲开。”
“一旦有旁观者在场，你这辈子都习惯了迎着危险往上顶。”
克莱尔狠狠地瑟缩了一下，仿佛被这句话当众扇了一个耳光。
丹尼尔大步走到冰箱上方的吊柜前，一把扯出那把信号枪，再次掰开枪管。他抠出那枚铝制的空弹壳，重重地砸在流理台上。
那是一枚单发式船用求救信号弹。它的设计初衷，是让燃烧的强光在几英里外都能被看到。在一个封闭的室内发射这玩意儿，它随时可能点燃地毯、窗帘，甚至直接引燃丹尼尔的衣服。刚才那一击，距离实木大书架不到一英尺。
他用两根手指捻着那枚空弹壳，不停地转动。
“大门有监控。” 他冷冷地说。
露丝摇了摇头。“今天早上电力系统闪断过一次。我不确定录像机有没有自动重启。”
“本地存储硬盘有内置的电池备用系统。”
“但硬盘主机在你的办公室里。” 克莱尔提醒道。
丹尼尔看向女儿。
是啊。她的手机被锁在里面。那个存放文件的防火保险箱被锁在里面。那份缺失了一页的十一页修正案原件，也被锁在里面。就算大门监控还在运作，它最多只能拍下维罗妮卡气势汹汹地杀进大门，甚至拍下她溜到墙角剪断主光缆，但它绝对拍不到厨房里发生的这荒诞的一幕。早在两年前，因为霍华德疑神疑鬼地指责佣人们监视他，这座豪宅内部的所有摄像头就已经被悉数拆除。
丹尼尔扔下了那枚空弹壳。
“我们立刻报警。”
维罗妮卡的脸上面如死灰，纹丝不动。只有她的右手大拇指，在神经质地反复摩擦着食指的侧面。
“报啊，你倒是报啊。” 她冷笑着挑衅。
克莱尔看着父亲。“拿什么报？”
“我爬到屋顶天线那儿，能把蜂窝模块重启。”
“那你要留我们两个单独跟她待在一起？！”
“露丝带你进办公室，把门反锁死。”
“我的手机还在里面！”
“这也正是我让你们进去的原因。”
维罗妮卡突然转身朝客厅走去。
丹尼尔一把死死攥住她的胳膊。
她像触电一样猛地转过身，速度之快让克莱尔失声尖叫，但维罗妮卡并没有动手。她只是用力试图挣脱丹尼尔的铁钳。
“我要拿我的鞋。”
“你哪儿也别想去。”
“我的鞋就在沙发旁边。”
“你刚刚对着壁炉开了一发信号枪！”
“所以我现在想穿上我的鞋。”
这种荒诞的逻辑，简直让空气都窒息了。
露丝低头瞥了一眼维罗妮卡光着的脚丫。她的一侧脚后跟被晚宴高跟鞋的带子磨得血肉模糊，通红一片。
“我去帮她拿。” 露丝说。
“不行。” 丹尼尔断然拒绝。
露丝的表情瞬间变得强硬起来。
“在过去的半个小时里，我被你像使唤狗一样命令坐下、藏好、监视、拿东西、甚至要把自己反锁在房间里。现在，我要去给这位女士拿她的鞋。”
她毫不妥协地走向客厅。
维罗妮卡重新坐回了吧台椅上。
丹尼尔松开了她的胳膊。
克莱尔从水槽下面的柜子里翻出一个急救箱，小心翼翼地清理着发际线的血迹。当丹尼尔想伸手替她拿消毒棉片时，她却躲开了。
“我自己能行。”
“我知道。”
“那就别管我。”
他只能尴尬地收回手。
露丝拎着那双俗气的金色晚宴高跟鞋的绑带回来了，面无表情地扔在维罗妮卡脚边。
“谢谢。” 维罗妮卡说。
露丝连哼都没哼一声。
维罗妮卡套上鞋，当坚硬的后跟带勒住那块破皮的伤口时，她疼得龇牙咧嘴。她尝试调整了两次，最后无奈地放弃了，直接把带子踩在了脚底。
这个极具生活气息的微小动作，让丹尼尔感到一阵没由来的烦躁。一个刚刚拿着致命凶器轰击他客厅的疯女人，现在居然在娇气地顾忌一个磨破的水泡。他的怒火极度渴望她能保持那种纯粹的邪恶形象，但她身上残存的这种人性，却在不断瓦解他的愤怒。
他从玄关抽屉的暗格里摸出办公室的钥匙。
“克莱尔和露丝进办公室。我把维罗妮卡押到图书馆去，反锁上所有的对外大门。然后我去屋顶修信号。”
维罗妮卡猛地站起来。
“你无权非法拘禁我！”
“但我绝对有权阻止你靠近我的女儿。”
“这根本不是你的房子！”
“是啊，” 丹尼尔冷笑，“这似乎是今晚唯一一件，我们所有人都无法忘记的事实。”
他押着维罗妮卡穿过客厅。
房间里依然弥漫着刺鼻的焦糊味。刺鼻的烟雾在天花板下积聚，烟雾探测器上已经亮起了红色警示灯，但不知为何还没有触发警报。丹尼尔走过时顺手推开了两扇窗户。
维罗妮卡在白色真皮沙发旁停住了脚步，回头死死盯着壁炉。
“又怎么了？” 丹尼尔不耐烦地问。
“没什么。”
“今天晚上这个词已经被你滥用得毫无信用了。”
她抬眼直视他。
“克莱尔骗我说藏在花瓶里的那个信封，并不是里面唯一的秘密。”
克莱尔不知何时已经站在了厨房门口。
“你这话什么意思？”
维罗妮卡指着那堆陶瓷碎片。
“当花瓶碎裂的时候，我看到了金属的反光。”
丹尼尔立刻折返回壁炉前。
他蹲下身，用拨火棍小心翼翼地拨开陶瓷碎片。在一块巨大的弧形碎瓷片下面，赫然躺着一个被熏黑了一半的黄铜圆筒。它只有拇指大小。
露丝也凑了过来。
“我发誓，我从来没见过这东西。”
“你可是每个星期都要给它换水的。” 克莱尔质疑。
“我只负责换玻璃内管里的花！我从来没把这该死的花瓶大卸八块过！”
丹尼尔捡起那个圆筒。一端有一个极细的螺纹盖。
维罗妮卡在碎片的另一侧单膝跪下。
“别碰任何东西。” 丹尼尔警告。
她充耳不闻，指着圆筒的一端。
“看那儿。”
一小截白色的纸边，从螺纹盖的缝隙里倔强地露了出来。
丹尼尔拧开了盖子。
里面塞着一张卷得极紧的米色纸条，厚重的黄铜外壳保护它免受了信号弹的烈焰吞噬。他小心翼翼地把它抽了出来。纸条在卷起之前曾被纵向对折过，边缘已经泛起了岁月的黄斑。
那不是什么缺失的见证人签名页。
那是霍华德亲笔写下的一张字条。
丹尼尔一眼就认出了那种极具压迫感、向右下角倾斜的字迹，还有那些写得过于用力的大写字母——那是因为霍华德在老派的寄宿学校里，但凡写错一个字就会被老师用戒尺狠狠抽打指关节而留下的肌肉记忆。
露丝，
如果丹尼尔赶在你之前发现了那份修正案，他一定会打着道德的幌子，把一个简单的利益问题上纲上线成一桩不可饶恕的丑闻。但如果是维罗妮卡先发现它，她绝对会不择手段地把一个没有法律约束力的口头承诺，当成讹诈我的致命武器。把那份附加的“知情同意书”藏好，直到他们两个都山穷水尽、愿意主动交代自己到底背着我干了什么见不得人的勾当为止。
H.
在字条的底部，赫然标着一个日期：霍华德去世前的第十二天。
克莱尔越过丹尼尔的肩膀看清了上面的内容。
“什么‘知情同意书’？”
露丝手里的玻璃杯猛地砸在流理台上。
杯子没有碎。它倒在台面上，咕噜噜地滚了一圈，将剩下的冰水肆意漫流在昂贵的大理石上。
没有人去管它。
维罗妮卡缓缓站直了身体。
“原来东西在你手里。”
露丝死死地盯着霍华德那张诛心的字条。
丹尼尔听见湖面上的寒风倒灌进敞开的窗户里，发出凄厉的呜咽。
“露丝。” 他低声唤道。
她从羊毛开衫的口袋里掏出一块手帕。有那么一瞬间，丹尼尔以为她要用它去擦拭台面上的水渍。但她没有。她把手帕死死地捂在了自己的嘴上。
## 第六章
“我万万没想到那个花瓶会被打碎。” 她闷声说。
维罗妮卡猛地朝她逼近了一步。
丹尼尔立刻像一堵墙一样挡在她们中间。
“那份‘知情同意书’到底在哪儿？”
露丝的视线依然死死粘在那张字条上。
“霍华德非要管它叫那个名字。那其实是他签署修正案之后，口述的一份补充声明。他说他必须把这一切白纸黑字地写下来，以证明他完全清楚自己刚刚干了什么，以及为什么要这么干。”
“是一份证明他具备完全行为能力的医疗声明吗？” 克莱尔问。
“不。不是那种东西。”
“那它现在到底在哪儿？”
露丝缓慢地叠起手帕。
“在我的房间里。”
维罗妮卡发出一声极其短促的声音，听起来像是在笑，又像是在嘲弄。
丹尼尔感到一股久违的怒火直冲脑门。这一次，愤怒的情绪无比纯粹，因为它太熟悉了。
“你把它偷偷藏了整整六个月！”
“是的。”
“你眼睁睁地看着信托委员会在法庭上把维罗妮卡的索赔要求撕得粉碎！”
“是的。”
“你眼睁睁地看着我对律师团队信誓旦旦地保证，绝对没有任何证据表明霍华德真的希望那份修正案生效！”
露丝傲然抬起下巴。
“你对律师说的话，可不止这些。”
“我还说了什么？！”
“你暗示他们，那份修正案极有可能是霍华德在神志不清、被恶意诱导的情况下签署的废纸。”
“我当时就是这么深信不疑的！”
“不，你只是‘极度渴望’它是那样的一张废纸！”
这句话像一记重锤，砸得空气都颤抖了一下。
丹尼尔看着露丝，仿佛他们之间横亘的十七年光阴，在这一刻被彻底重置了。
她第一次见到他时，他才二十五岁，刚刚新婚。那时的他不过是个穿廉价西装的初级物业助理，习惯把老板的每一个指令都事无巨细地记在一个黑色的小笔记本里。是露丝手把手地教他：哪几扇红木门在潮湿的夏天会卡壳，哪几位信托董事在晚宴上喝多了会发酒疯，以及当霍华德居高临下地要求你提供“建议”时，你该如何用最卑微的措辞把“绝对服从”包装成他想要的答案。
在克莱尔出生的那个兵荒马乱的夜晚，是因为丹尼尔在病床前吓得晕了过去，是露丝第一个把刚出生的克莱尔抱在怀里。
在丹尼尔妻子安娜（Anna）漫长的化疗期间，因为霍华德极其蛮横地把董事会安排在同一天，而当时的丹尼尔还天真地以为“随叫随到”等于“忠心耿耿”，是露丝整夜整夜地守在安娜的病床前。
而在霍华德的葬礼结束后，也正是这个露丝，眼睛都不眨地看着丹尼尔的脸，赌咒发誓说她对那神秘消失的最后一页一无所知。
“为什么？” 他沙哑地问。
露丝的嘴角绷成了一条线。
“因为我答应了霍华德的嘱托。”
“嘱托你销毁证据？！”
“嘱托我按兵不动！”
“等什么？！”
“等你们两个中的任何一个，良心发现，主动说出真相。”
维罗妮卡的声音尖锐得刺耳：“我从头到尾说的都是真话！”
露丝转头看着她。
“不，你没有。”
维罗妮卡再次咄咄逼人地往前迈了一步。
丹尼尔猛地抬起一只手：“退后！”
“她到底以为我干了什么伤天害理的事？！”
露丝的目光像刀片一样，扫过那件香槟色的睡袍、里面那件奢华的晚礼服，以及她散乱的长发。
“你当初死皮赖脸地留在这里，根本不是因为你无家可归。”
维罗妮卡脸上的表情瞬间被抽干了。
克莱尔在他们两人之间来回扫视。
露丝冷酷地继续扒皮：
“霍华德早就查清了你那堆烂账。”
“这在这个圈子里根本不算什么秘密。”
“他知道你背着他，偷偷把你在城里的高档公寓抵押了出去。”
“那是我的私有财产！”
“他也知道你打着他的旗号，在外面招摇撞骗去骗贷款。”
丹尼尔猛地转向维罗妮卡。
她死死地瞪着露丝。
“你这是血口喷人！”
“贷款公司直接把核实电话打到了霍华德的私人专线上。”
“他当时亲口答应过他们会做我的担保人！”
“但他连一个字的担保文件都没签过。”
“他在电话里向他们承诺了！”
“他对很多人都许下过很多不切实际的承诺。”
维罗妮卡的防线终于在这一瞬间崩溃了。“你凭什么觉得，当他的承诺对你有益时，你就可以用他生病来博取同情；而当他的承诺损害了你的利益时，你就可以轻易地把他当成一个疯子打发掉？！”
露丝的脸颊狠狠地抽搐了一下。
维罗妮卡敏锐地捕捉到了这个痛点，乘胜追击。
“你冷眼旁观他一步步滑向痴呆的深渊，然后你借机把自己包装成了他生命里唯一不可或缺的救世主！每次他忘记了什么，你总是第一个跳出来，添油加醋地告诉他他‘原本’的意思是什么。每次他改变了主意，你就用‘老糊涂了’来全盘否定。你把掌控他的记忆，变成了你在这座房子里作威作福的特权！”
露丝的眼眶瞬间通红，但她硬是没有掉一滴眼泪。
丹尼尔彻底挡在了她们中间。
“够了！”
“不够。” 克莱尔突然开口。
所有人都看向她。
她双手死死地攥着霍华德留下的那张残破字条。
“这根本不够。你们只是在比谁的嗓门更大而已。”
她转向露丝。
“维罗妮卡到底干了什么？”
露丝深吸了一口带着焦味的空气。
“她花言巧语地骗霍华德，从他的私人账户里私自划走了整整二十万美金，去填补她自己那些见不得光的投资窟窿。”
维罗妮卡拼命摇头。
“是他主动提出来的！”
“而你却恬不知耻地让他以为，这笔钱在一个月内就能还上。”
“那本来就是打算要还的！”
“你还了吗？”
